newsitem.title: UK: UK bankers welcome regulatory change, want details.
newsitem.headline: UK bankers welcome regulatory change, want details.

text.p: British bankers welcomed changes in the industry's regulatory structure announced earlier on Tuesday by Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown but said they were keen to see the full details of the plan.

"We welcome the rationalisation of the financial services area and support the SIB being given appropriate powers," said Sir William Purves, chairman of Britain's biggest banking group HSBC Holdings, which owns Midland Bank.
Purves said efforts to eliminate costly duplication of regulation, a sore point with many bankers, were to be applauded.

Brown said that responsibility for the regulation of the banking industry would pass from the Bank of England to an enlarged Securities and Investments Board (SIB) to be chaired by current deputy governor of the central bank, Howard Davies.
But the Bank will maintain a role since Brown has given it overall responsibility for the stability of the financial system.
Peter Ellwood, chief executive of Lloyds TSB Britain's largest retail financial services group, said he was supportive of the moves because they reflected what was happening in the market.

"Most financial institutions are now selling banking and insurance products," Ellwood said. "Therefore this will be a cleaner, tidier and better arrangement for regulators, financial institutions and the consumer."

The move to a unitary regulatory authority came as no real surprise. But Brown again, after his stunning move just after the May 1 election to give the BOE charge of interest rate policy, surprised the financial community with the pace at which he is introducing change.
Both Brown and his Treasury colleague Alistair Darling had made clear in the run-up to the election that they had radical changes in mind.

The Bank of England has come in for heavy criticism for its supervision of the banking system in the wake of the failure and fraud at Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI), which was closed in 1991 with debts of over $12 billion, and the collapse of British merchant bank Barings in 1995 when trading losses of 800 million pounds ($1.3 billion) wiped out its capital.

In the wake of the Barings affair, the bank commissioned a report by an outside firm of consultants and moved to bolster its regulatory regime to try and avoid a repetition through its Review of Banking Supervision.
As recently as March, the Bank put forward a new regulatory framework which was designed to take more account of individual risk situations and risk controls.
Tuesday's move also brought a welcome from the British Bankers' Association.

"This is a bold move and we clearly need to see more detail," said its director-general Tim Sweeney. "We look forward to working with the authorities to make this work in the interests of London as an international financial centre and the UK financial services sector as a whole."
Sweeney said he hoped the new regime would maintain two aspects of the role of the Bank which had always been valued.

"First, that its supervisors are close to the markets they supervise; second, that it has been a consultative system, making supervisory policy more effective. We will be looking for this to continue."

The Bank took on the formal role of banking supervisor in 1979 under the Banking Act which was partly inspired by the fringe banking crisis of 1970s when many small depositors lost money and by a European directive which called on member states to institute a licensing scheme for banks which had previously not existed in Britain.

Before then, regulation of banking was carried out by the traditional raising of the Governor's eyebrows which consisted mainly in pointing out to institutions that if they followed a certain course, the wrath of the Bank would be expressed in an appropriate way. ($ = 0.608 British Pounds)
